item.title: 100 Objects #25: Beaded Moccasin
item.description:
Poet Sarah Kay grew up with a pair of moccasins framed on the dining room wall. She didn’t know much about the beautiful, soft leather shoes with intricate beadwork, except that they had been a gift to her grandmother, June Suzuki, from a student when she taught at a boarding school for Native American children back in the 1940s. June worked there soon after she was released from an internment camp for Japanese-Americans during WWII. Sarah thought this was just a strange, but unrelated series of events. But when Sarah started delving deeper into her grandmother’s story, she discovered a dark current in US history connecting the two events… and a surprising revelation about her grandmother.

A History of the United States in 100 Objects is a production of 99% Invisible and BBC Studios.

item.title: Know the Score
item.description:
A credit score is essentially a three digit number that here in the US usually ranges from 300-850. It's a metric that lenders can use to predict your ability to pay back a loan. The higher the number, the more likely you are to be approved for lines of credit. In the United States, your credit score decides where you can live, what car you can drive and whether you can get a loan. It’s supposed to be objective—a precise, omniscient accounting of your financial health, but what started as a simple tool for lenders ended up embedding itself in the lives of most Americans, and feeding the same bias it claimed to solve.

item.title: 100 Objects #24: White House Solar Panels
item.description:
In 1979, President Jimmy Carter took to the roof of the White House to announce the installation of 32 solar panels. In that speech, he outlined all the things that they could become: a curiosity, a museum piece, one of our nation's most potent and enduring symbols of a road not taken, or the start of a great adventure. They would become all but the last of those things…but why? Journalist and environmental activist Bill McKibben takes Roman Mars through the story of how a president showed the American people a powerful new technology promising abundant cheap energy and why Americans shrugged.

A History of the United States in 100 Objects is a production of 99% Invisible and BBC Studios.

item.title: Perfectly Leveraged for the Squat
item.description:

item.title: 100 Objects #23: Coin From the Ship of Gold
item.description:
On August 20th, 1857 a ship set sail from the Port of San Francisco with 600 people and thousands of pounds of gold. That gold was destined for the vaults of New York City banks, but it never made it. Instead, the ship sank to the bottom of the ocean, taking all that gold with it. Executive Producer Annie Brown sits down with Roman Mars to tell the story of the sinking of the SS Central America and the gold that sparked the first global financial panic, helped fuel the Civil War, and—over a century later—ruined one man’s life.

A History of the United States in 100 Objects is a production of 99% Invisible and BBC Studios.

item.title: 100 Objects #22: AOL Disc
item.description:
In 1998, the recording industry was thriving. But the company pressing more compact discs than anyone else in America wasn't a record label…it was an internet company: America Online. The AOL Disc was a marketing coup—hugely successful. It’s not an overstatement to say that it’s the campaign that introduced America to the internet. Because of how well it worked, for a while the internet was AOL. And then… it felt like AOL just disappeared. So what happened? Alex Goldman (Reply All, Hyperfixed) finds out.

A History of the United States in 100 Objects is a production of 99% Invisible and BBC Studios.

item.title: Doktoro Esperanto
item.description:
Esperanto is what linguists call a “constructed language.” It isn’t attached to a nation or a region, and it didn’t evolve from another language over time. Instead, nearly 150 years ago, someone decided to sit down and design the whole thing from scratch. 

That someone was L. L. Zamenhof, also known as Doktoro Esperanto. He created this language with the hope that it would unite the world under one shared tongue. Today, reporter Katie Thornton tells the story of Doktoro Esperanto’s dream, and what we can all still learn from Esperanto right now.

For more, check out Katie's story on Esperanto in Harper's Magazine.

item.title: 100 Objects #21: Window from the House of D
item.description:
In 1932, the Women's House of Detention—New York City's first women's prison—opened in the heart of Greenwich Village. It was opened to make "wayward" women quiet, private, and properly feminine. And the building had one unique feature originally meant to be a sort of kindness—a special kind of window that the women inside could open. Roman Mars and historian Hugh Ryan trace how those special windows had an impact that nobody could have predicted—helping to build a mecca of gay America and, ultimately, a movement.

item.title: Audio Guide of the Imperfections of a Perfect Masterpiece
item.description:
This episode is sponsored by Acura.

From the outside, the building is a light gray spiral, and from the inside, the art is displayed on one long ramp that curves up towards a glass skylight in the ceiling. We’re going to take the greatness of this building as a given. What we’re going to focus on are the oddities, the accretions, the interventions that reveal a different kind of genius. Not just the genius of Frank Lloyd Wright, and his bold, original vision, but the genius of all the people that made this building function, adapt, and grow over the decades.

item.title: 100 Objects #20: AA Sobriety Chip
item.description:
Comedian, writer, and podcaster Jamie Loftus has always known about Alcoholics Anonymous. As a kid, she loved the album where her dad kept all his AA chips — that little piece of plastic that marks a day, a month, a year of sobriety. Now as an adult, Jamie wanted to understand where that little chip came from. What she found is that imbued in that little chip is a hidden history — from Prohibition to women’s suffrage — of America’s relationship to gender, religion, and morality.

A History of the United States in 100 Objects is a production of 99% Invisible and BBC Studios.

As a kid, she loved the album where her dad kept all his AA chips — that little piece of plastic that marks a day, a month, a year of sobriety. Now as an adult, Jamie wanted to understand where that little chip came from. What she found is that imbued in that little chip is a hidden history — from Prohibition to women’s suffrage — of America’s relationship to gender, religion, and morality.

item.title: 100 Objects #19: Western Electric 500 Series
item.description:
This episode is sponsored by Claude. For problems worth solving, get started with Claude at Claude.ai.

The Western Electric 500 Series Telephone used to be everywhere. For over 50 years, it was the default telephone for homes, offices and literally anywhere else you might need a phone… but how did that happen? Why was this one phone so much better than everything that came before… or, in some ways, since? Former MythBuster Adam Savage joins Roman Mars to explore the history of the 500 Series Telephone and what we lost when we eventually decided to leave it behind.

item.title: 100 Objects #18: Hair Relaxer
item.description:
Somewhere between 85 to 95 percent of Black women in the United States have used a chemical hair relaxer at least once in their lifetime. It is a ubiquitous American product with a complicated legacy: it built Black wealth and opened economic doors, but also taught generations to see their hair as a problem to be solved. And now research is revealing a physical cost. Roman Mars and producer Priscilla Alabi explore how a single product became a mirror for all of America's contradictions.

A History of the United States in 100 Objects is a production of 99% Invisible and BBC Studios.

item.title: 100 Objects #17: M43 Field Jacket
item.description:
Articles of Interest host Avery Trufelman joins Roman to tell the incredible story of the American military’s jacket problem: How should the military outfit its soldiers to make them as safe and effective as possible? The answer was the M43 Field Jacket, which not only changed what it meant to be a soldier and look like a soldier, it changed what we all wear every day—in America, and around the world.
